new_items.title: A single-cell and spatial 3D multi-omic atlas of developing human basal ganglia
new_items.summary_rss: Single-cell and spatial profiling of the developing human basal ganglia show that their principal neurons, spiny projection neurons, mature through unusually synchronized epigenomic remodeling; that oligodendrocytes pass through a transient chromatin state during differentiation; and that spiny projection neurons carry an elevated genetic risk for schizophrenia and bipolar disorder.

new_items.title: An integrative single-cell epigenomic atlas annotates the regulatory genome of the adult mouse brain
new_items.summary_rss: A comprehensive single-cell epigenomic atlas integrates four histone modifications, chromatin accessibility, DNA methylation, the 3D genome, and the transcriptome, and resolves functional chromatin states of the adult mouse brain. This integrative framework, together with sequence-based deep learning, identifies active and repressive regulatory mechanisms and their dynamic deployment underlying cell-type-specific gene regulation.

new_items.title: Circuit-aligned specialization of human basal ganglia astrocytes
new_items.summary_rss: Astrocyte diversity in the human basal ganglia reflects both large-scale brain identity programs and local microcircuit specialization. Integrated transcriptomic, epigenomic, and spatial analyses link these astrocyte populations to subgroup-specific regulatory features and enhancer logic, providing a framework for understanding and targeting astrocyte heterogeneity.

new_items.title: Collaboration across scales: More than the sum of its parts
new_items.summary_rss: Science is collaborative by nature, but some questions require coordination on an exceptional scale. Among them is the challenge of creating a comprehensive reference framework for the human brain. In this issue of Cell, together with papers published in Cell Genomics, Cell Reports, Cell Reports Methods, Cell Systems, and Neuron, we present the first publication package from the NIH BRAIN Initiative Cell Atlas Network (BICAN).

new_items.title: Common variation of cell abundances and gene expression in the human striatum
new_items.summary_rss: Single-cell analyses of the adult human striatum and prefrontal cortex reveal substantial inter-individual variation in cell-type abundance and gene expression. Most aspects of donor-associated cellular and molecular features recur across brain regions, while age and common genetic variation have distinct effects across cell types.

new_items.title: Conserved striatal mechanisms underlying ASD
new_items.summary_rss: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) involves changes in social and stereotypic behaviors regulated by striatal circuitry. Using an innovative cross-species approach, in this issue of Cell, Yuan et al. identify alterations in specific striatal neurons and astrocytes, opening new avenues for investigating cellular and molecular mechanisms underlying striatal dysfunction in ASD.

new_items.title: Cross-species multiomic atlas of the primate basal ganglia
new_items.summary_rss: A cross-species multiomic atlas of the primate basal ganglia aligns 1.8 million nuclei from human, macaque, and marmoset into 61 cell types conserved over 76 million years. The atlas reveals that dorsal-ventral spatial identity is more evolutionarily constrained than direct and indirect pathway or striosome and matrix identity, identifies a distinct SMYD2-HTR7 spiny projection neuron type, and links regulatory sequence grammars and psychiatric risk variants to specific cell populations.

new_items.title: Deploying liquid intelligence in cancer: Finding answers in our blood
new_items.summary_rss: Liquid biopsies provide a noninvasive way to screen for disease. This review explains how AI-powered multimodal foundation models will help to identify robust tumor signals from liquid biopsies at scale, but clinical and infrastructural hurdles will need to be addressed to deliver their promise to the clinic.

new_items.title: Disruption of cell-type-specific molecular programs of striatal spiny projection neurons in autism
new_items.summary_rss: Cross-species single-cell profiling identifies molecular disruptions among striatal spiny projection neurons in genetically defined autism. D1 striosome spiny projection neurons are identified as the most affected, with altered synaptic and energy metabolism programs linked to reduced EGR1/EGR3 activity, partly reproduced by EGR1/EGR3 loss in organoids.

new_items.title: From the human genome to the human brain cell atlas
new_items.summary_rss: The BRAIN Initiative Cell Atlas Network (BICAN) is establishing an evolving reference for neuroscience by integrating cell identities, anatomy, and multimodal evidence across species. In analogy with the Human Genome Project, the BICAN basal ganglia atlas is a model for a federated reference to advance understanding of brain organization, function, variation, and disease.

new_items.title: Harmonized brain ontology and 3D atlases for human, macaque, and marmoset basal ganglia
new_items.summary_rss: A Harmonized Ontology of Mammalian Brain Anatomy (HOMBA) enables consistent creation of structural and cellular brain atlases and ontologies as well as the integration of multimodal data and samples across species.

new_items.title: Mapping primate brain aging across cell types, regions, and sexes
new_items.summary_rss: Aging is the major risk factor for neurodegenerative disease, yet how it affects different cells in the primate brain remains unclear. In this issue of Cell, Yang et al. present a single-nucleus atlas of the aging macaque brain that, together with recent work by Zhang et al., reveals context-dependent aging programs, sex-biased transcriptional aging, and molecular links to Alzheimer’s disease.

new_items.title: Mesoscale molecular architecture of the striatum across cell types and adult aging
new_items.summary_rss: Using Slide-tags spatial transcriptomics across 19 human donors, this study shows that the striatum is organized into six molecularly distinct zones that are conserved in macaque and mouse, align with brain-wide projection inputs, and lose their transcriptional distinctiveness with age.

new_items.title: Morphoelectric diversity and specialization of primate striatal neuron types
new_items.summary_rss: Patch-seq in the macaque striatum links transcriptomic cell-type identity to neuronal form and function, revealing non-canonical spiny projection neurons, specialized interneurons, spatially organized morphoelectric gradients, and features that distinguish macaque from mouse neuron types.

new_items.title: Multimodal single-cell epigenomic and 3D genome atlas of the human basal ganglia
new_items.summary_rss: A single-cell atlas of DNA methylation and 3D genome architecture across the human basal ganglia defines the regulatory signatures of its cell types, including a distinct striatal projection neuron subtype, and predicts cell-type-specific gene regulatory networks. Spatial transcriptomics further reveals interneuron types that differ between the striatal matrix and striosomes.

new_items.title: Multiscale spatial atlas of human basal ganglia cell types and communities
new_items.summary_rss: This study combines MERFISH+ and Stereo-seq to generate a multiscale spatial transcriptomic atlas of the human basal ganglia. It reveals cellular community organization, conserved and species-specialized features of striosome-matrix architecture, and projection-associated molecular signatures inferred from subcellular RNA localization.

new_items.title: Single-cell analysis of chromatin state and transcriptome in the human basal ganglia
new_items.summary_rss: A single-cell multi-omic atlas spanning eight regions of the human basal ganglia maps cell-type-specific chromatin landscapes and gene regulation, revealing the regulatory programs that shape cell identity. The atlas provides a framework for interpreting noncoding variants linked to basal ganglia traits and diseases, and it enables the construction of a deep-learning model for predicting how variants affect gene regulation and function.

new_items.title: Single-cell multimodal atlas reveals regulatory programs in the human brain
new_items.summary_rss: A multimodal, integrative framework for understanding gene regulatory mechanisms across diverse cell types in the adult human brain. This framework helps elucidate how regulatory programs govern neuronal and glial functions, encode developmental trajectories, underlie neurological phenotypes, and change during evolution.

new_items.title: Single-cell, multi-region profiling of the macaque brain across the lifespan
new_items.summary_rss: Yang, Watkins et al. generate a 5.3 million cell transcriptomic atlas of the aging primate brain, which reveals that glia drive most age-related compositional shifts. These data uncover region-, cell-type-, and sex-specific molecular trajectories linked to neurodegenerative disease, providing key insights into the cellular mechanisms underlying brain aging and vulnerability.

new_items.title: Spatial and regulatory organization of cell identity across the primate subcortex
new_items.summary_rss: Dense multimodal profiling of the marmoset subcortex reveals how spatial context and gene regulatory programs jointly shape cell identity across the primate brain. By linking transcriptional states, chromatin accessibility, and anatomy, this atlas uncovers regulatory principles underlying spatial gradients, neuronal convergence, and evolutionary specialization.

new_items.title: Spatial transcriptomics reveals molecular organization of human and nonhuman primate basal ganglia
new_items.summary_rss: A cellular-resolution spatial transcriptomics atlas of the basal ganglia in human, rhesus macaque, and common marmoset highlights a conserved molecular organization and introduces an accessible resource for the research community. This atlas reveals complex gene expression gradients that coexist with discrete cell-type specializations.

new_items.title: Stepping (hi)stones: Charting a single-cell multiomic path toward understanding the human brain
new_items.summary_rss: In this issue of Cell, two single-cell multiomic atlases jointly profile transcription and histone modifications across different regions of the adult human brain, revealing cell-type-specific regulatory landscapes, developmental epigenetic memory, and improved interpretation of neurological variants. These studies establish a framework for understanding human brain cell identity, evolution, and pathology.

new_items.title: Toward an integrated framework for a human and mammalian brain cell atlas
new_items.summary_rss: The BRAIN Initiative Cell Atlas Network integrates molecular profiles, spatial maps, and anatomical frameworks into a curated cell-type taxonomy of the human, macaque, and marmoset basal ganglia. This multimodal atlas offers a blueprint for comparing brain cell types across species and for scaling to the whole brain.

new_items.title: COP1 is a temperature-responsive switch in Arabidopsis.
new_items.summary_rss: Temperature is molecular motion, but how living systems sense this is poorly understood. Many responses in plants integrate light and temperature signals, for example, via light receptors and the circadian clock. CONSTITUTIVE PHOTOMORPHOGENESIS 1 (COP1) regulates light signaling and is necessary for responding to temperature. We show that COP1 acts as a temperature-dependent switch, becoming activated by a warm temperature-induced conformational change. An intramolecular Val-Pro (VP) motif binds to the active site of COP1 at low temperatures, preventing substrate docking. At warmer temperatures, the VP motif becomes detached, enabling client proteins to bind and be degraded. This discovery explains how plants are able to obtain a precise readout of temperature within a given climate range. Altering the binding of the VP motif is sufficient to adjust the temperature range within which the plant responds. This helps us understand how plants are able to adapt to different climates.

new_items.title: Nicotianamine-driven nickel transport to sink organs underpins maize productivity.
new_items.summary_rss: Nickel (Ni), the last essential trace element identified in plants, has long been enigmatic regarding the genetic basis underlying its homeostasis and its agricultural significance. Using genome-wide association analysis, we identified ZmNAET1 as a key transporter controlling Ni allocation to seeds. Mechanistically, ZmNAET1 mediates nicotianamine secretion and enables nicotianamine-dependent phloem loading of Ni in nodes and subsequent Ni translocation into sink organs. Mutants lacking ZmNAET1 exhibit significant yield penalties, decreased seed germination velocity, and drastically shortened seed longevity. In an irreplaceable role, supplemented Ni fully rescued seed germination and proper vegetative development of the mutants. We show that NAET1-dependent delivery of Ni to urease is essential for amino acid turnover in developing sink organs, revealing an unappreciated role of Ni in yield formation of graminaceous plants. This study uncovers an underestimated requirement for nicotianamine and Ni and opens a new research avenue toward optimizing micronutrient provision for cereal crop productivity.

new_items.title: Reconstructing developmental and disease progression with sample-level embeddings.
new_items.summary_rss: Single-cell genomics is transformative for characterizing cellular heterogeneity, but many biological questions require comparing samples rather than individual cells. Typical analyses compare "case" and "control" groups, ignoring sample-level variation within them. Here, we present scSLIDE (single-cell sample-level inference using density estimation), a framework that transforms each sample's single-cell data into a compact profile describing where its cells are distributed in high-dimensional space. By comparing these density profiles, scSLIDE calculates embeddings to characterize variation across samples. We implement scSLIDE in version 6 of our Seurat package and apply it to COVID-19 infection, Alzheimer's disease, and zebrafish embryogenesis. scSLIDE reveals patient subgroups, reconstructs disease trajectories, and identifies coordinated cellular programs across samples. We discover separable axes of infection and severity, a trajectory of Alzheimer's progression, and embryonic "pseudostages" that vary across and within time points. Our results demonstrate how case-control analyses collapse rich biological variation into binary labels and how sample-level embedding represents a powerful analytical alternative.

new_items.title: The blood-brain barrier imports diverse neuroprotective proteins through pathways impaired early in Alzheimer's disease models.
new_items.summary_rss: The blood-brain barrier (BBB) has been defined primarily by what it excludes, yet the scale and function of physiological blood-to-brain protein transport remain largely unknown. Using bioorthogonal proteomics, we find that the healthy BBB samples 191 plasma proteins and permits 92 into the brain parenchyma. Enriched for carrier and metabolic functions, these proteins home to distinct brain cell types, such as apolipoprotein A1 (APOA1) to astrocytes and alpha-1 antitrypsin (SERPINA1) to microglia. This cell-type tropism relies on a BBB-parenchyma receptor hand-off: APOA1 crosses the BBB via SR-B1 and engages astrocytic ATP-binding cassette transporter A1 (ABCA1), a key Alzheimer's risk gene, driving cholesterol efflux that supports synapse integrity. Unlike LPS-induced nonspecific leakage, early-stage 5xFAD mice show selective BBB transport remodeling, with reduced APOA1 and increased SERPINA1 uptake. Hepatic APOA1 overexpression restores APOA1 in the 5xFAD brain, rescuing astrocytic, synaptic, and behavioral deficits. These findings recast the BBB as a selective interface that recruits neuroprotective circulatory proteins for brain health.

Melting and resistivity of iron at Earth core conditions using pulsed Joule heating.
new_items.summary_rss: The melting temperature and electrical resistivity of iron at high pressure are essential for understanding Earth's core. Here we use a new high-pressure method - microsecond pulsed Joule heating in diamond anvil cells - to identify melting and measure resistivity of solid and liquid iron. More than 300 reproducible melting measurements indicate a surprisingly shallow melting curve, reaching 6 K/GPa and 4160 ± 80 K at 200 GPa. Extrapolating in pressure and iron alloy composition, and combining with our 76 [Formula: see text] cm measurement of liquid iron's resistivity, we infer a relatively cold core-mantle boundary (3430 K) with a low adiabatic outer core heat flow (9.8 TW). This suggests thermal convection alone could have powered the geodynamo prior to inner core formation and that today's lowermost mantle is fully solid.
